english: to grill / to roast / to bake
usage: The default verb for Korean BBQ — at a 고깃집 you 고기를 구워 먹어요 (grill and eat the meat yourself).
Same verb covers oven-baking: 빵을 굽다, 쿠키를 굽다. Korea doesn't split 'bake' vs 'grill' like English.
examples: 삼겹살은 제가 구울게요.
I'll grill the pork belly.
구울게요 (ㅂ-irregular + 을게요) is what you say when you volunteer to man the grill.
고기 다 구웠어요?
Is the meat all grilled?
Super common table question. 구웠어요 is the ㅂ-irregular past — note it's NOT 굽었어요.
김 좀 더 구워 주세요.
Please grill some more seaweed.
구워 주세요 — asking staff or a friend to cook a bit more for you.
nuance: 굽다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb, so the ㅂ turns into 우 before vowel endings: 구워요, 구웠어요, 구울 거예요. It's the single most useful cooking verb for a foreigner in Korea because Korean BBQ (구이) is everywhere, and the same word also means oven-baking bread or roasting. Don't say 굽어요 — that's a classic learner error.
mistakes: Saying 굽어요/굽었어요 instead of the ㅂ-irregular 구워요/구웠어요.
Using 굽다 for boiling or frying in oil — those are 삶다/끓이다 and 튀기다.

english: to stir-fry / to pan-fry (with little oil)
usage: Stir-frying old kimchi (김치볶음밥, 볶음김치) is a staple home dish — 볶다 implies tossing in a hot pan with a bit of oil.
Use 볶다 for quick high-heat tossing; the noun form 볶음 names dishes like 제육볶음, 오징어볶음.
examples: 밥이랑 김치 넣고 같이 볶아요.
Put in the rice and kimchi and stir-fry them together.
Classic 김치볶음밥 instruction — 볶아요 for the tossing action.
채소를 센 불에 빨리 볶았어요.
I stir-fried the vegetables quickly on high heat.
센 불 = high heat, the natural collocation with 볶다.
기름 두르고 마늘부터 볶을까요?
Shall we coat the pan with oil and stir-fry the garlic first?
볶을까요? — suggesting a cooking step to someone cooking with you.
nuance: 볶다 is a regular verb (볶아요, 볶았어요) and means stir-frying or pan-frying with a small amount of oil over high heat, constantly moving the food. It's distinct from 튀기다 (deep-frying in lots of oil) and 부치다 (pan-frying flat things like 전/jeon). Tons of restaurant dish names end in 볶음 (제육볶음, 낙지볶음), so recognizing this verb helps you read menus.
mistakes: Confusing 볶다 (stir-fry, little oil) with 튀기다 (deep-fry, lots of oil).
Using 볶다 for pancake-style frying — that's 부치다 (e.g. 전을 부치다).

usage: 삶다 = cooking a solid food IN boiling water (eggs, noodles, potatoes), as opposed to 끓이다 (boiling a liquid/soup).
When you cook pasta or 칼국수, you 면을 삶아요. The pronunciation is [삼따] — the ㄹ in ㄻ is silent here.
examples: 계란 몇 분 삶아요?
How many minutes do you boil the eggs?
Everyday kitchen question; 삶아요 keeps the ㅏ vowel (NOT 삶어요).
감자를 푹 삶았어요.
I boiled the potatoes until soft.
푹 삶다 = boil thoroughly/until tender, a very natural collocation.
국수 삶을게요, 양념장 만들어 주세요.
I'll boil the noodles, please make the sauce.
삶을게요 — splitting kitchen tasks with someone.
nuance: 삶다 means to boil a solid food by submerging it in water — eggs, noodles, potatoes, vegetables, even towels for sanitizing. It contrasts with 끓이다, which is boiling a liquid or making soup/stew. The ㄻ batchim takes a vowel ending (삶아요, 삶았어요), and is pronounced [삼]. A frequent mistake is reaching for 끓이다 when you really mean 삶다.
mistakes: Using 끓이다 (boil a liquid/soup) when you mean 삶다 (boil a solid food in water).
Writing 삶어요 — the verb stem vowel is bright (ㅏ), so it's 삶아요.

usage: 찐만두 (steamed mandu) vs 군만두 (fried) — the verb tells you the cooking method on the menu.
찐 고구마 is a beloved snack. 찌다 = cook with steam, keeping food moist.
examples: 만두 좀 쪄 줄 수 있어요?
Could you steam some dumplings?
쪄 (찌다 contracts ㅣ+어 → ㅕ) is the form learners often get wrong.
호박을 살짝 쪘어요.
I lightly steamed the zucchini.
쪘어요 = past of 찌다; 살짝 (lightly/briefly) pairs naturally with steaming.
같이 떡 찔까요?
Shall we steam rice cakes together?
찔까요? — suggesting steaming as the cooking method.
nuance: 찌다 contracts ㅣ + 어 into ㅕ, giving 쪄요 and 쪘어요 — a spot where beginners often write 찌어요 by mistake. It means cooking by steam, which keeps food moist; you'll see it as the 찐- prefix on menus (찐만두, 찐빵, 찐 옥수수). Note this is a homonym of the 찌다 in 살이 찌다 ('to gain weight'), so context matters.
mistakes: Writing 찌어요/찌었어요 instead of the contracted 쪄요/쪘어요.
Confusing 찌다 (steam) with the identical-looking 찌다 in 살이 찌다 (gain weight).

usage: 튀기다 = cook submerged in hot oil. The noun 튀김 names dishes like 새우튀김, 야채튀김.
Always implies a lot of oil and high heat, unlike 볶다 (stir-fry with a little oil).
examples: 새우를 바삭하게 튀겼어요.
I deep-fried the shrimp until crispy.
바삭하게 (until crispy) is the classic result phrase for 튀기다; past is 튀겼어요.
감자튀김 직접 튀겨 먹어요.
I deep-fry french fries myself.
튀겨 먹다 = fry (something) and eat it; common 'cook-it-yourself' pattern.
기름 뜨거우니까 튀길 때 조심하세요.
The oil is hot, so be careful when deep-frying.
튀길 때 = when deep-frying; a natural safety reminder.
nuance: 튀기다 is a regular verb (튀겨요, 튀겼어요) for cooking food submerged in plenty of hot oil. Keep it separate from 볶다 (stir-fry, little oil, constant tossing) and 부치다 (shallow pan-fry flat foods). The 튀김 noun form is everywhere in markets and 분식 shops, so recognizing the verb helps you order. It's also used for 'to bounce' a ball, but the cooking meaning dominates in daily life.
mistakes: Mixing up 튀기다 (deep-fry, lots of oil) with 볶다 (stir-fry, little oil).
Spelling it 튀기다 but conjugating as 튀기어요 — the correct contracted form is 튀겨요.

english: to boil (a liquid) / to make (soup, stew, ramyeon)
usage: The set phrase for cooking instant ramyeon. Koreans never say 라면을 만들다 for cooking it — it's always 끓이다.
끓이다 = bring a liquid to a boil or simmer a soup/stew (찌개를 끓이다, 국을 끓이다).
examples: 라면 끓여 줄까요?
Shall I make you some ramyeon?
끓여 줄까요? — offering to cook ramyeon, an extremely common everyday line.
된장찌개를 끓였어요.
I made soybean-paste stew.
끓이다 is THE verb for making any 찌개/국; past 끓였어요.
물 먼저 끓일게요.
I'll boil the water first.
끓일게요 — announcing your next cooking step.
nuance: 끓이다 is the causative pair of 끓다 ('to be boiling'): you 끓이다 a liquid to make it 끓다. Use it for boiling water and, crucially, for making soups, stews, and ramyeon — 라면을 끓이다 is fixed usage. The key contrast for learners is 삶다 (boil a solid food in water) vs 끓이다 (boil a liquid / make a brothy dish). Conjugates regularly: 끓여요, 끓였어요.
mistakes: Saying 라면을 만들다 instead of the natural 라면을 끓이다.
Using 끓이다 to boil eggs or noodles — that solid-in-water sense is 삶다.

usage: Step one of most 나물 side dishes: quickly boil greens, then drain and season (무치다).
데치다 always means a SHORT dunk in boiling water — 살짝 데치다 is almost redundant but very common.
examples: 콩나물을 살짝 데쳤어요.
I quickly blanched the bean sprouts.
데쳤어요 = past of 데치다 (ㅣ+어 → ㅕ); pairs with 살짝.
브로콜리는 끓는 물에 데쳐 주세요.
Please blanch the broccoli in boiling water.
끓는 물에 데치다 = the standard blanching instruction.
나물 데칠까요?
Shall I blanch the greens?
데칠까요? — offering to do the blanching step.
nuance: 데치다 means a quick blanch — dropping vegetables (or sometimes squid) into boiling water for just seconds to soften them and lock in color, then draining. It's a prep step, not full cooking, and is the gateway to Korean 나물 banchan: 데치다 then 무치다 (season). Don't confuse it with 데우다 (to reheat already-cooked food), which sounds similar but is unrelated. Conjugates 데쳐요, 데쳤어요.
mistakes: Confusing 데치다 (blanch in boiling water) with 데우다 (reheat food).
Treating 데치다 as full boiling — it's only a brief dunk; longer cooking is 삶다/끓이다.

english: to season and toss (by hand) / to dress (a salad/namul)
usage: The defining verb for Korean side dishes: mix blanched greens with 양념 by hand. 무침 (the noun) names dishes like 오이무침, 골뱅이무침.
무치다 means coating an ingredient evenly with sauce/seasoning, usually by hand or tongs.
examples: 시금치를 참기름에 무쳤어요.
I dressed the spinach with sesame oil.
무쳤어요 = past; 참기름에 무치다 is the quintessential namul finish.
오이 좀 새콤하게 무쳐 주세요.
Please dress the cucumber to be tangy.
무쳐 주세요 — asking someone to season-toss it; 새콤하게 = tangy.
콩나물 데쳐서 무칠까요?
Shall we blanch the bean sprouts and then season them?
데치다 + 무치다 = the standard two-step for banchan; 무칠까요? proposes the step.
nuance: 무치다 is the hands-on tossing that finishes most Korean banchan: you blanch (데치다) a vegetable, then 무치다 it with seasoning until evenly coated. The noun 무침 labels a whole category of cold seasoned dishes (무침류) on menus. Conjugates 무쳐요, 무쳤어요. Don't mix it up with 비비다 (to mix by stirring, like bibimbap) — 무치다 specifically means dressing/coating, often by hand.
mistakes: Confusing 무치다 (season/dress by tossing) with 비비다 (stir/mix together).
Spelling it 뭍이다 or similar — the verb is 무치다, conjugated 무쳐요.

english: to slice / to cut (food, on a board)
usage: 썰다 is the cooking-specific 'cut' — slicing food on a cutting board (도마). More natural than 자르다 in the kitchen.
Pairs with size adverbs: 얇게 썰다 (thinly), 어슷썰다 (on a diagonal), 송송 썰다 (into thin rounds).
examples: 대파를 송송 썰어 주세요.
Please slice the green onion into thin rounds.
송송 썰다 = mince into little rounds, a set kitchen phrase; 썰어 주세요 to ask for it.
고기를 한입 크기로 썰었어요.
I cut the meat into bite-sized pieces.
썰었어요 = past (ㄹ stem keeps ㄹ before 어); 한입 크기 = bite-size.
제가 양파 썰까요?
Shall I slice the onions?
썰까요? — the ㄹ drops before ㄹ/ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ, hence 썰까 (not 썰을까).
nuance: 썰다 is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the ㄹ disappears before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings (썹니다, 써세요) but stays before vowel endings (썰어요, 썰었어요). In the kitchen 썰다 is far more natural than the general 자르다 (already in your deck) for slicing food on a board. Learn it with the cutting adverbs — 얇게, 채 썰다 (julienne), 어슷, 송송 — which appear constantly in recipes.
mistakes: Keeping the ㄹ in front of ㅂ/ㅅ — it's 썹니다 and 써세요, not 썰습니다/썰으세요.
Using 자르다 for everything; in cooking, slicing food is more naturally 썰다.

usage: 다진 마늘 (minced garlic) is in almost every Korean recipe; you can even buy it pre-minced at the mart.
The past-attributive 다진 + noun is how you describe pre-minced ingredients: 다진 고기, 다진 양파, 다진 마늘.
examples: 마늘이랑 양파를 잘게 다졌어요.
I finely minced the garlic and onion.
잘게 다지다 = mince finely; 다졌어요 is the past.
생강도 좀 다져 주세요.
Please mince some ginger too.
다져 주세요 — asking for an ingredient to be minced.
다진 고기로 동그랑땡 만들까요?
Shall we make patties with the minced meat?
다진 고기 = ground meat; shows the attributive form in real use.
nuance: 다지다 means chopping something into very fine pieces — finer than 썰다. It shows up constantly as the attributive 다진 (다진 마늘, 다진 고기) in recipes and on product labels, so it's worth recognizing even before you cook much. Conjugates regularly: 다져요, 다졌어요. The same verb metaphorically means 'to firm up / consolidate' (기초를 다지다), but the kitchen sense is what you'll use daily.
mistakes: Confusing 다지다 (mince, very fine) with 썰다 (slice into pieces).
Forgetting the attributive 다진 — say 다진 마늘, not 다지는 마늘, for 'minced garlic'.

english: to mix together (by stirring) / to rub
usage: 비비다 is the verb hiding in 비빔밥 — you 밥을 비벼 먹어요, stirring rice with toppings and gochujang.
Outside the kitchen, 비비다 means rubbing two surfaces together (눈을 비비다, 손을 비비다).
examples: 고추장 넣고 잘 비벼서 드세요.
Add gochujang and mix it well before eating.
비벼서 드세요 = mix it and then eat; the standard bibimbap instruction.
참기름 넣고 비볐어요.
I added sesame oil and mixed it.
비볐어요 = past of 비비다 (ㅣ+어 → ㅕ).
비빔국수 같이 비빌까요?
Shall we mix the spicy noodles together?
비빌까요? — proposing to do the mixing; note the pun-like 비빔/비비다 pairing.
nuance: 비비다 means mixing by stirring and tossing everything together — it's literally the root of 비빔밥 and 비빔국수. The key contrast for cooks is 비비다 (stir everything together evenly, like bibimbap) vs 무치다 (dress/coat an ingredient with seasoning, usually a side dish). It conjugates regularly (비벼요, 비볐어요) and also means 'to rub' (눈을 비비다) in non-food contexts. A super practical word at any Korean table.
mistakes: Confusing 비비다 (stir/mix together) with 무치다 (season/dress an ingredient).
Writing 비비어요 instead of the contracted 비벼요.

english: to cool (something) down / to let cool
usage: 식히다 is the causative of 식다 ('to cool off'): you 식히다 hot food so it 식다. Useful before serving kids or eating.
it's hot, so let it cool before eating
식혀서 먹다/드세요 is an everyday caretaking phrase you'll both hear and say.
examples: 국이 너무 뜨거우니까 좀 식혀서 드세요.
The soup is too hot, so let it cool a bit before eating.
식혀서 드세요 — telling someone to let it cool; pairs with 뜨겁다.
빵을 한 김 식혔어요.
I let the bread cool for a moment.
한 김 식히다 = let the steam/heat off briefly; 식혔어요 is the past.
커피 좀 식힐까요?
Shall I cool the coffee down a bit?
식힐까요? — offering to cool a hot drink before someone drinks it.
nuance: 식히다 is the causative/transitive partner of 식다: 식다 means food cools by itself, while 식히다 means you actively cool it (blowing on it, leaving it out, fanning it). It conjugates regularly (식혀요, 식혔어요) and is genuinely useful at the table — telling someone 식혀서 드세요 ('let it cool before eating') is caring and natural. Don't mix it with 식다, which can't take an object.
mistakes: Using intransitive 식다 with an object — say 국을 식히다, not 국을 식다.
Confusing 식히다 (cool down) with 시키다 (to order food / make someone do) — similar sound, totally different meaning.
